slides.title: Debugging Embedded Programs
slides.subtitle: ENGS 28 · Day 7x — In-Class
slides.presenterNote: 50 minutes, self-contained, no pre-class reading. Students arrive mid-Lab-4. Show the settling notice while people sit down.

slides.title: While we settle
items: Open your old Blinky project in STM32CubeIDE.
Click build. Leave it compiling in the background.
You will need it, built and healthy, in about 15 minutes.
slides.presenterNote: Repeat this out loud once. Moving the project-reopen tax here is what keeps Part 3's launch to 8 minutes.

slides.title: Today
items: What the compiler is trying to tell you
The debugger, hands-on: watch a register change

slides.title: Where Do Bugs Come From?
slides.presenterNote: ≈ 6 min. Show of hands over the list — keep your own hand up throughout. Then 60 s of writing: which habit would have caught yours? If long: drop the write-and-share, keep the hands (cut order step 1, −2 min).

slides.title: Finding Bugs Without New Tools
slides.presenterNote: ≈ 9 min, two predict-then-reveal cycles. Students commit answers in writing BEFORE each reveal. If long: 2b's predict becomes a told reveal (cut order step 2, −3 min).

slides.title: One thing is wrong with this Blinky
The Debugger, Hands-On
slides.presenterNote: ≈ 24 min: 8 launch / 5 IOPENR / 4 MODER / 7 breakpoints. Say out loud: 'a good number of these won't launch on the first try — that's normal, put your hand up and I'll come by.' CHECKPOINT minute 32: if the room is not mostly past IOPENR, the MODER moment happens on the projector and Part 3d becomes a student-driven front demo. Never cut Part 3 itself.

slides.title: If it will not launch
slides.presenterNote: Sit on this slide while circulating. blinky.c is on Canvas — confirm before class. Recovery is: download, paste over Src/main.c, build (~60 s). If that fails too, pair them up; do not spend launch time resurrecting a project.

slides.title: This is what you should see
Predict, then step
slides.presenterNote: The crucial step. Each student writes their own prediction before their own Step Over — do not gate the room. You are circulating; the slides are the pace.

slides.title: Why is MODER not zero?
slides.presenterNote: Let the puzzle land before advancing — a beat of silence, then take guesses.

slides.title: The reference manual (RM0490 §6.4.1), watched live
slides.presenterNote: The datasheet moment. The PA13/PA14 punchline is told, not derived.

slides.title: Step both lines: audit the write
Breakpoints: set a destination
slides.presenterNote: Anyone done early goes straight to the stretch on their own ADCPot.c — say it here at Part 3d, not at minute 47.

slides.title: Watch a Variable Change
slides.presenterNote: ≈ 5 min. Default: all-hands — everyone predicts, then presses, on their own machine. Pressed for time? Switch to demo mode from the front (see the instructor slide); if very long: a 90-second demo (cut order step 3).

slides.title: Reminder: demo mode if pressed for time
Break when this happens
slides.presenterNote: If you might switch to demo mode: stage the podium machine before class — counter built, board wired, CoolTerm connected on the right port, no old debug session running.

slides.title: Predict, then press
slides.presenterNote: Keypress only after the prediction is written. Answer: 117 = 0x75.

slides.title: Which Tool, When
slides.presenterNote: ≈ 3 min, then the rest of the hour is Lab 4 with the debugger open.

slides.title: The rest of the hour: Lab 4, with the debugger open
items: A paused chip is not real time, so timing questions go to the scope. More on that when interrupts arrive.
Stretch: watch ADC_DR move as you turn the pot; audit ADC_CHSELR and ADC_CR against your init code.
Launch never worked today? Every step and screenshot is in the chapter. Redo it on your own before next class, and ask for help if it still will not connect.
